headline: High: shared shell/filesystem and overlapping write/network capabilities create default risks of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors between the two open-source agents.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write the filesystem and use stdin/stdout, so one can place content the other may later ingest as trusted input. ms-swift also handles datasets, logs, and configuration files; the course agent uses notebooks and a LangGraph subagent model, making output-to-input bridging plausible even without a documented shared channel.
conditions: IF the two agents share a workspace directory or exchanged files, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF either agent parses file or notebook content as instructions, attacker-controlled text can steer behavior.
mitigations: Separate working directories per agent.
Disable automatic ingestion of peer-generated files.
Add provenance labels to all exchanged artifacts.
Review notebook inputs before execution.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization at the handoff boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both profiles touch files and secrets: ms-swift handles hub_token/sdk-token and the course agent handles JINA_API_KEY, TELEGRAM__BOT_TOKEN, and Langfuse keys. With shared filesystem access and allowlisted egress, either agent could expose sensitive material through logs, notebooks, or API calls. The pairwise leak path is plausible in default local development setups.
conditions: IF both agents run in the same local workspace, secrets can be read from shared files.
IF either agent logs or forwards file contents to its backend/API, sensitive data can leave the environment.
mitigations: Store secrets in separate per-agent env files.
Rotate exposed tokens before co-running.
Mount read-only inputs where possible.
Redact logs and notebook outputs.
requires-engineering: isolate network and filesystem namespaces per agent.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and allowlisted network egress. Neither profile states locking or coordination, and ms-swift explicitly does not support multiple instances while the course agent does. Concurrent writes to shared files, notebooks, or configs can corrupt state or overwrite work, so the conflict is dangerous by default if co-located.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, write conflicts are reachable.
IF either agent mutates shared configs or generated artifacts without locks, state corruption can occur.
mitigations: Use separate output directories.
Run only one writer per shared resource.
Add file locks around mutable artifacts.
Snapshot the workspace before execution.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: The course agent’s LangGraph subagent model and API endpoints suggest it may consume upstream outputs, while ms-swift can generate training/evaluation artifacts and configuration data. If B treats A’s outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream notebook runs or agentic actions. No verification or provenance controls are stated, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text, configs, or evaluation outputs as inputs, errors can propagate.
IF B’s notebooks or API flows act on A’s artifacts without validation, downstream mistakes become likely.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before reuse.
Validate schemas on all exchanged artifacts.
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default.
Compare outputs against source data.
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware gating between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents handle secrets and potentially sensitive content, but only B explicitly requests Docker Desktop and Airflow credentials while A handles hub/sdk tokens. The profiles do not show a clear residency mismatch or regulated-data class like PHI, so this is a policy-mismatch risk rather than a breach certainty. The other agent is cited because the compliance issue arises from their combined handling of secrets and logs.
conditions: IF either agent stores secrets in shared logs or notebooks, retention policy mismatch becomes relevant.
IF the deployment crosses organizational boundaries, access-control and residency review is required.
mitigations: Document secret-retention rules for both agents.
Keep audit logs separate.
Avoid placing regulated data in shared notebooks.
Review credential scopes before launch.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows across systems.
